newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks shed disdain, seek to woo investors.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks shed disdain, seek to woo investors.

text.p: Stung by criticism that they treat investors with disdain, big Japanese banks are beginning to woo potential shareholders with investor relations campaigns.

"Bank management is changing. Six months ago one couldn't imagine that the president of a big bank would join analysts' meetings," Yoshinobu Yamada, a financial analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc, said on Tuesday.

Analysts keen to know how financial firms will cope with Japan's "Big Bang" reforms aimed at boosting competition in the long-protected sector got a rare sample of top management thinking earlier this week when Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) president Masao Nishimura met them for a chat.
Sumitomo Bank Ltd also took the investor relations plunge in late May, when its president-to-be Yoshifumi Nishikawa chaired a similar gathering. Nishikawa formally assumed his new post on June 27.
It was the first time Sumitomo had met with analysts to explain its financial situation and management strategy.

Other banks such as Sanwa Bank Ltd and Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd have explained their financial conditions to analysts in the past, but the presence of top executives has a strong appeal, analysts said.

"It is good for the president to explain his management policy directly to us, since he is the final decision-maker," said an analyst at a European brokerage. "In the past, in regulated markets, banks only paid attention to the Finance Ministry, but now they have begun to look to investors."

Kouya Hasegawa, an analyst at Nikko Research Center, said that banks have been interested in investor relations campaigns to keep share prices from falling in the wake of vague worries about the banking sector, which has been reeling from a massive problem loan mess.

Those fears have repeatedly put pressure on bank shares in recent years as confidence in Japan's financial system has weakened due to a series of financial institution failures, because of the problem loans, since 1995.
Some Japanese firms took tentative steps to improve investor relations in the early 1990s after Tokyo share prices slumped.

But banks have remained targets of criticism for their low profitability and their reluctance to disclose key data, including exposure to problem loans -- a legacy of their aggressive lending policy in the late 1980s bubble economy of inflated asset prices.
The prospect of solving the problem loan mess and the prospect of intense competition as Japan reforms its financial sector, however, have prodded big bankers to change their attitudes.

Last month, Japan unveiled a blueprint for a drastic programme to break the barriers separating the nation's various financial sectors and to deregulate those markets two years ahead of an original goal of 2001.

The reform plan is kicking off just as a huge scandal involving racketeer payoffs by brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd and a major commercial bank, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd, have reinforced doubts about corporate governance and ethics at the nation's financial institutions.
Many financial experts, meanwhile, doubt Japan's stodgy banks will become world-class competitors in global markets.
And some investor relations campaigns have left some pressing questions unanswered.

"Many Japanese banks say that they are aiming to boost ROE (return on equity) and capital adequacy ratios. But their targets are still low compared with Western rivals and it is not clear yet how they will achieve the targets," said one analyst.
